canonical_statement: The review compared the efficacy and adverse-event profiles of available GLP-1 receptor agonist therapies for adults with type 2 diabetes using systematic review and network meta-analysis.
The review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO as CRD42022342845.
The report followed PRISMA 2020 and the PRISMA extension for network meta-analysis.
PubMed, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and Embase were searched from inception, with the search updated on 17 December 2022 and 19 August 2023 after the initial 9 July 2022 search.
Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults with type 2 diabetes comparing a GLP-1 receptor agonist with placebo or another GLP-1 receptor agonist for at least 12 weeks.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes in randomized controlled trials
inclusion_criteria: GLP-1 receptor agonist versus placebo or GLP-1 receptor agonist

canonical_statement: The review excluded crossover trials, non-inferiority trials comparing a GLP-1 receptor agonist only with another drug class without placebo, withdrawn GLP-1 receptor agonists, and non-English reports.

population.label: Candidate randomized trials
exclusion_criteria: non-inferiority comparison against another drug class without placebo

canonical_statement: Two reviewers independently extracted trial data and a third reviewer adjudicated disagreements.

Primary outcomes were change from baseline in HbA1c, fasting blood glucose, and body weight; secondary outcomes included BMI, waist circumference, HDL-C, LDL-C, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and adverse events.
When continuous-outcome standard deviations were unavailable, the investigators imputed or borrowed standard deviations from similar randomized trials as described in the methods.
Values presented only in figures were digitized with WebPlotDigitizer.
Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2.

Network meta-analysis used a frequentist random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood in Stata MVMETA; continuous outcomes were summarized as mean differences and binary adverse events as odds ratios.
Treatment rankings were summarized using SUCRA values.
Local inconsistency was assessed with node splitting and global inconsistency with a design-by-treatment interaction approach.
Confidence in network estimates was evaluated with CINeMA.
Publication bias was assessed with comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger and Begg tests where applicable.
Sensitivity analyses added otherwise eligible active-comparator trials that lacked a placebo arm and also used leave-one-out analyses.
Meta-regression evaluated patient age, diabetes duration, and background glucose-lowering therapy as potential effect modifiers.
Prespecified subgroup analyses examined drug dose, follow-up duration, and single versus dual/triple receptor agonism.
The final quantitative synthesis included 76 randomized controlled trials with 39,246 participants and 15 GLP-1 receptor agonist treatments.

population.label: Included randomized controlled trials

canonical_statement: A total of 16,316 records were identified; after 2,673 duplicates, 13,643 records were screened, 483 full texts were assessed, and 76 trials entered the quantitative synthesis.
Taspoglutide was excluded from the review because its development had been discontinued after gastrointestinal adverse effects.
Sixty-eight of 76 trials (89%) were judged low risk for random sequence generation.

population.label: Included randomized trials

concept.text: Low risk for random sequence generation

canonical_statement: Ten of 76 trials (13%) were judged high risk of bias overall.

population.label: Included randomized trials

canonical_statement: The investigators reported no strong global inconsistency for most outcomes, although some local node-splitting inconsistency was present.
The investigators reported no high heterogeneity and described most pairwise CINeMA comparisons as moderate or high confidence.
Comparison-adjusted funnel plots and formal tests did not show clear evidence of small-study effects or publication bias.
Sensitivity analyses that added active-comparator trials and leave-one-out analyses were reported as consistent with the primary findings.
Meta-regression did not identify significant modification of the primary outcomes by age, diabetes duration, or background treatment.

canonical_statement: The supplementary appendix contains 17 appendices covering database search strategies, study characteristics, extracted data, risk of bias, inconsistency/heterogeneity, secondary outcome networks, rankings, league tables, CINeMA, funnel plots, sensitivity analyses, meta-regression, dose comparisons, dose subgroup analyses, follow-up subgroups, receptor-class subgroups, and dose-specific adverse events.
Appendix 8 is titled as league tables for a network meta-analysis of 75 trials, whereas the main article reports 76 randomized trials in the final quantitative synthesis.
The supplementary appendix reuses the label “Table S4” for both an Embase search strategy table and a risk-of-bias table, creating a source-internal table-numbering collision.
Clinical and methodological heterogeneity across populations and follow-up durations could reduce precision of pooled network estimates.
Diet and exercise were not adequately controlled across included trials.
Some randomized trials did not report enough detail on randomization, allocation concealment, or blinding despite attempts to obtain further information.
Several GLP-1 receptor agonists were represented by relatively few trials, limiting certainty for some comparisons and subgroup analyses.
Some included trials were open-label and industry funded, creating potential bias.

The authors concluded that all included GLP-1 receptor agonist therapies improved glycaemic outcomes versus placebo, with tirzepatide showing the greatest glycaemic efficacy and CagriSema the largest body-weight reduction.
The authors cautioned that gastrointestinal adverse effects, particularly at higher doses, should be considered when selecting GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy.
